Under no circumstances should you jump from heights, use elevators, or try to run down stairs while the ground is shaking.
tips.benefit: Recommended actions include “using hands or soft objects to shield the head and neck” and “gripping table legs tightly”; if no table is available, “crouch close to load-bearing walls and stay away from exterior walls, windows, and balconies.” For those outdoors, the advice is “immediately move to an open area away from hazards.” Conversely, during the 1988 Armenian earthquake, Soviet-era prefabricated panel buildings collapsed en masse. A case-control study conducted after that disaster concluded that “leaving a building right after the first tremor is a protective behavior.” People who remained indoors were 4.40 times more likely to sustain injuries than those who evacuated (95% CI 2.24–8.71). The odds of injury indoors were 12.20 times higher than outdoors (3.62–63.79), and in buildings five stories or taller, this risk rose to 3.65 times that of lower structures (2.12–6.33).
tips.sources: Armenian HK, Noji EK, Oganesian AP (1992). A case-control study of injuries arising from the earthquake in Armenia, 1988. Bulletin of the World Health Organization, 70(2), 251-257. Mahue-Giangreco M, Mack W, Seligson H, Bourque LB (2001). Risk factors associated with moderate and serious injuries attributable to the 1994 Northridge Earthquake. Annals of Epidemiology, 11(5), 347-357. <https://doi.org/10.1016/s1047-2797(01)00220-4>
tips.caveats: This topic remains debated, as the two main conclusions apply to distinctly different types of buildings. In Armenia, entire buildings collapsed, leaving no safe spot to hide, so evacuation was the only viable option. The U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency advises residents to “drop to the ground, protect the head and neck, hold on tight, and avoid running outside” — where injuries are primarily caused by falling debris and falls during tremors. Research from the Northridge earthquake further shows that reaching for objects or gripping seemingly stable items can actually increase injury risk. Ultimately, the key question isn’t “should I run or stay?” but rather “is this building likely to collapse, and can I reach open ground within seconds?” For buildings constructed after 2001 that require navigating stairs or hallways to exit, staying put is the safest choice. For single-story homes, older brick buildings, and makeshift houses without seismic protection, the exit is just a few steps away — so leave immediately. It’s worth noting that the Armenian study only compared injured and uninjured survivors, excluded fatalities, and didn’t account for differences in building height; since those able to escape were more likely to live on lower floors, these figures should be interpreted with some caution. Under no circumstances should you jump from heights, use elevators, or attempt to run down stairs during tremors. Once outside, stay far away from tall structures, overpasses, utility poles, glass facades, and billboards.

tips.title: When encountering bears, wild boars, or packs of wild dogs, don’t run, don’t scream, don’t make eye contact — instead, turn sideways and back away slowly.
tips.cost: No cost involved. When heading into the mountains, bring a hiking pole, hike in a group, and make noise so animals know you’re coming. The hardest part is staying put instead of running.
tips.inPlainWords: Never run — bears can sprint uphill or downhill just as fast as racehorses. Also, don’t climb trees; both black bears and brown bears are excellent climbers. Stand your ground and keep speaking to the bear in a low, calm voice. Once it stops moving, turn sideways and back away slowly. If a brown bear attacks, lie down and play dead: place your hands behind your neck and spread your legs apart. For black bear attacks, do not play dead — run toward a vehicle or building; if escape is impossible, fight back using whatever is at hand. In case of dog bites, follow the steps outlined in item 13.
tips.benefit: The original guidelines issued by the U.S. National Park Service on bear encounters contain six key points: “Do not run — bears can sprint uphill or downhill just as fast as racehorses.” “Stay calm; most bears have no interest in attacking and simply want to be left alone.” “Keep speaking to the bear in a low, steady voice.” “When the bear stops moving, turn sideways and back away slowly so you can keep watching it without tripping.” “Make yourself appear as large as possible.” “Do not climb trees — both grizzly bears and black bears are capable climbers.” In the event of a brown bear attack, “lie down and play dead, placing hands behind the neck and legs apart.” For black bear attacks, “do not play dead; run toward a vehicle or building, and if escape is impossible, fight back using any available object.” Dog bites should be treated according to item 13.
tips.sources: US National Park Service. Staying Safe Around Bears. <https://www.nps.gov/subjects/bears/safety.htm>
tips.caveats: The Grade B rating applies solely to bear encounters. Never try to lure animals with food, approach them for photos, or bring dogs into mountainous areas inhabited by wild boars.

tips.title: If caught in a thunderstorm outdoors, get into a hard-topped vehicle or building; avoid ridges, lone trees, water surfaces, and metal objects
tips.cost: No monetary cost. The downside is that your trip gets interrupted for at least half an hour. The real challenge is actually turning back when the thunder is still far away.
tips.inPlainWords: There is no safe spot outdoors during a thunderstorm. You must get into a hard-topped vehicle or building; convertibles and motorcycles do not qualify. Tents, gazebos, areas under trees, or rocky outcrops also do not count as shelter. Stay away from open areas, mountain ridges and peaks, isolated tall trees, water surfaces, and metal railings or poles. If a group cannot all fit together, spread out rather than huddling close. Begin retreating the moment you hear thunder; it is only safe to leave 30 minutes after the final clap of thunder.
tips.benefit: There is no safe spot outdoors during a thunderstorm. It is only safe to leave 30 minutes after the final clap of thunder.
tips.sources: National Weather Service. Outdoor lightning safety: "There is no safe place outside when thunderstorms are in the area" "Avoid open fields, the top of a hill or a ridge top. Stay away from tall, isolated trees or other tall objects" "Stay away from water, wet items, such as ropes, and metal objects, such as fences and poles"; "If you are in a group, spread out to avoid the current traveling between group members"; Resume activity "Wait 30 minutes until after the last rumble of thunder". <https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-outdoors>
tips.caveats: Tents, gazebos, areas under trees, and rocky outcrops do not qualify as shelters. Hard-topped cars do count, but convertibles and motorcycles do not. Start retreating the instant you hear thunder; do not wait until rain begins to fall.

tips.title: Gradually increase your sleeping altitude when heading to high elevations; if symptoms worsen, descend immediately — don’t tough it out.
tips.cost: It requires an extra day or two for acclimatization. Preventive medications are prescription-only, so you must consult a doctor before traveling. The main challenge is fitting these days into an otherwise tight itinerary.
tips.inPlainWords: This guideline focuses on sleeping altitude, not daytime elevation. Sleeping above 2,450 meters already poses a risk of altitude sickness. Once above 3,000 meters, you should only raise your nighttime altitude by 500 meters per night, allowing an additional day of acclimatization for every 1,000-meter increase. Symptoms such as headache, nausea, unsteady gait, altered mental state, or shortness of breath even at rest indicate the need to descend. Descending takes priority over oxygen therapy or medication.
tips.benefit: Sleeping above 2,450 meters increases the risk of altitude sickness. Without prompt descent, high-altitude cerebral edema and pulmonary edema — fluid buildup in the brain and lungs — can be fatal.
tips.sources: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Yellow Book High Altitude Travel and Altitude Sickness: "Any unacclimatized traveler proceeding to a sleeping altitude of ≥2,450 m (≥8,000 ft)—and sometimes lower—is at risk for altitude illness"; Ascent rate "500 m (1,650 ft) per night in sleeping altitude once above 3,000 m (9,800 ft)" 1000 meters plus acclimatization day; Acetazolamide prophylaxis "125 mg twice a day; 250 mg twice a day if >100 kg body weight"; "If symptoms become worse despite rest or treatment at the same elevation" must be withdrawn. <https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/environmental-hazards-risks/high-altitude-travel-and-altitude-illness.html>; Wilderness & Environmental Medicine (2024). Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Prevention, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Acute Mountain Sickness (2024 Update). Wilderness & Environmental Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wem.2023.05.013>
tips.caveats: The rule specifically refers to sleeping altitude, not daytime elevation. Headache, nausea, unsteadiness, confusion, or breathlessness at rest are clear signs to descend. Descending should always come before oxygen use or medication; continuing upward while on oxygen is unsafe.

tips.title: To remove a tick, use fine-point tweezers to pull it straight out along the skin — don’t apply oil, don’t use heat
tips.cost: A pair of fine-point tweezers.
tips.inPlainWords: Use fine-point tweezers to grasp the tick’s head right against the skin, then pull steadily outward. Never apply oil, use heat, or yank sideways — doing so can force infectious fluids into the skin and often leaves the tick’s mouthparts embedded. After removal, write down the date. If you develop fever, rash, or fatigue in the following weeks, be sure to mention the tick bite to your doctor.
tips.benefit: Applying oil, using heat, or pulling sideways can provoke the tick to release infectious fluids into the skin. Those actions also raise the risk of leaving its mouthparts stuck inside. From 2010 through 2024, the average fatality rate stood at 4.79%, rising with age; for those over 85 it reached 9.15%.
tips.sources: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. After a tick bite: "Grasp the tick as close to the skin's surface as possible using clean fine-tipped tweezers" "Pull tick away from the skin with steady, even pressure" "Do not use petroleum jelly, heat, nail polish, or other substances to try and make the tick detach from the skin. This may agitate the tick and force infected fluid from the tick into the skin". <https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/after-a-tick-bite/index.html>
tips.caveats: Be sure to note the date of removal. Should fever, rash, or fatigue appear in the weeks that follow, inform your doctor about the tick bite — otherwise it may be misdiagnosed as a common cold.

tips.title: Always boil any water taken from the wild before drinking it; one minute of boiling is sufficient — there’s no need to extend the time just because you’re at high altitude.
tips.cost: You’ll need to carry extra weight in the form of a stove and fuel.
tips.inPlainWords: Any microbes capable of causing illness through water are killed within seconds at boiling temperature. Boiling for an additional minute simply provides a safety margin for any possible oversight; it isn’t necessary to prolong the process at higher elevations. If boiling isn’t feasible, use a filter or chemical purification tablets instead — each method has its own limitations regarding which pathogens they can eliminate. Even crystal-clear streams and meltwater can harbor parasites.
tips.benefit: All microbes that can cause disease via water are inactivated within seconds at boiling temperature. The belief that water fails to reach a safe temperature at high altitudes is a common misconception.
tips.sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Yellow Book Travelers' Water Disinfection: "All organisms that may cause illness from drinking water are killed within seconds at boiling temperature" "CDC recommends that travelers boil water for a full minute to account for user variability in identifying boiling points and to add a margin of safety" "Although the boiling point for water decreases with increasing elevation, at common travel elevations the temperature needed to achieve boiling is still well above the temperature required to inactivate enteric pathogens". <https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/preparing-international-travelers/water-disinfection-for-travelers.html>
tips.caveats: The same page also notes that boiling isn’t strictly mandatory: maintaining water at 60°C for 30 minutes achieves the same effect, and boiling simply offers a visible endpoint without needing a thermometer. Filters and chemical tablets each have their own gaps in pathogen coverage, so boiling remains preferable when possible. Just because water appears clear doesn’t mean it’s free of parasites — appearance alone is no reliable indicator.

tips.title: If a stranger demands money in a remote area, hand over cash, avoid any confrontation, note their features, and call police after escaping
tips.cost: The cash you have on you. The real challenge is keeping your temper in check.
tips.inPlainWords: Give him the money, do not fight back, and do not argue. By demanding a few hundred rupees, he is committing robbery — a crime punishable by at least three years up to ten years in prison. If he enters a residence, uses a weapon, or causes serious injury or death, the sentence rises to ten years or more, even life imprisonment or death. If you chase after him and strike him after he has taken the money, that is no longer considered self‑defence. Immediately after escaping, write down his appearance, accent, vehicle license plate, and the direction he fled, then call 112.
tips.benefit: Your life is far more valuable than a few hundred rupees. The offender is committing a serious crime for such a small amount. Article 20 limits self‑defence to stopping an ongoing unlawful attack; once the robber has taken the money and walked away, any retaliation is no longer justified. After escaping, record his description, speech patterns, vehicle details, and escape route, then call 112.
tips.sources: National Disaster Management Authority. <https://ndma.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The “C” rating reflects the lack of direct literature supporting the principle that “handing over money avoids danger”; the legal text merely outlines the offender’s risks and your boundaries. Never follow an attacker to a secluded spot to “get money,” never reveal your phone password, and never get into his vehicle. This advice is not an invitation to fight or to refrain from calling police; it applies only when you are physically threatened in a remote setting and must first pay to ensure your safety. In contrast, if someone online threatens to release private photos or videos, you must never pay — see Section 8, Item 32 for those cases.

tips.title: If you stumble upon a group fight, walk away immediately — don’t try to break it up, don’t stand around watching, and don’t pick up any weapons on the ground. If you want to call the police, retreat to a safe distance and dial 112.
tips.cost: No money is required. The hard part is resisting the urge to step in and the temptation to watch from the sidelines. After calling, you might be asked to give a statement later; at most, this takes half a day.
tips.inPlainWords: If you intervene, your actions shift from “trying to calm things down” to “taking part in a fight.” Participating in a group brawl can land you in prison for up to three years; if many people are involved, it happens on a road, or weapons are used, the sentence rises to three to ten years. Watching isn’t worth it either — the more onlookers there are, the messier the scene gets, and you’re more likely to get hurt. The right move is to walk away. If you do want to call the police, step back to a safe spot and dial 112, clearly stating the location, how many people are involved, whether anyone is carrying knives or sticks, and if anyone has collapsed.
tips.benefit: If such fights cause serious injury or death, perpetrators are charged under laws on intentional injury or homicide. Group fights handled as hooliganism can lead to up to fifteen days in jail and fines up to ₹28,400. Guideline 5 of the “Opinions on Properly Applying Self‑Defence” says unlawful attacks include those aimed at you, at the public, or at others. Guideline 9 adds that if one side starts the fight with excessive force, or continues attacking even after the other side tries to avoid conflict, the responding party is usually considered acting in self‑defence.
tips.sources: National People’s Congress (2018). Criminal Procedure Law (revised in 2018, Articles 62, 110, 111, 193). Full text reproduced by the People’s Procuratorate of Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region <https://www.nx.jcy.gov.cn/zwsy/qwfb/202011/t20201119_608817.html>; National Disaster Management Authority. <https://ndma.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: This grade is B because part of the consequences are backed by clear legal text, but the advice “walk away and call the police instead of intervening” isn’t directly stated in any official rule — it’s inferred from those statutes and from how group fights are judged. Saying “I was just trying to mediate” isn’t a shield; what matters is whether you actually took part and whom you hit. If an attacker is already down or has fled, chasing them to hit them no longer counts as self‑defence. Legally, you may intervene if you see someone being unilaterally beaten; self‑defence protects not only you but also others. Yet stepping in bare‑handed usually just adds another casualty. Calling for help, recording from afar, and calling police are far more effective. The safest choice here is “don’t intervene, don’t watch.” The benefit of calling 110 mainly helps the victim on the ground; overall, this entry offers one of the lowest net benefits in the book, so you must weigh whether the time investment is worth it. You should know a few key facts first. There is already a legal duty to testify: Article 62 of the Criminal Procedure Law says anyone aware of a case must testify; not calling police doesn’t erase that duty. In cases involving serious injury or death, police can still identify witnesses from surveillance footage, so standing around watching actually makes you more likely to be recorded. Authorities “must keep the identity of anonymous callers confidential” (Article 111). Simply stating the location, number of people, and whether weapons are present is enough — you needn’t stay on the scene. Only if a court summons you to testify without a valid reason and you refuse can you face up to ten days in detention (Article 193); ordinary bystanders rarely reach that point. Two actions after walking away would cross the line: helping hide someone or giving false testimony to protect them (Article 310 of the Criminal Law, up to three years; serious cases bring three to ten years); and deliberately giving false testimony when called as a witness (Article 305, up to three years; serious cases up to seven years). Staying silent or telling the truth is fine; fabricating stories is not. If you yourself get caught in a fight, see Section 8, Item 10; if a stranger demands money, see Item 36 of this section; for costs after helping an injured person, see Item 39.

tips.title: If you may have been exposed to HIV, get PEP within 72 hours — the sooner, the better
tips.cost: A full 28‑day course of PEP can cost thousands of rupees; in most regions it must be paid out‑of‑pocket. You’ll need to rush to a hospital that same night. The hardest part is admitting you might be infected and leaving right away.
tips.inPlainWords: If you suspect you’ve been exposed to HIV, 72 hours is the hard deadline — ideally you should start PEP within 2 hours. The medication must be taken for 28 consecutive days. After 72 hours this option is no longer available, so don’t wait until the next day to decide.
tips.benefit: The Beijing Municipal Government’s HIV‑prevention outreach defines this as “post‑exposure prophylaxis,” abbreviated PEP. It recommends starting preventive medication “as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours and no later than 24 hours, but not after 72 hours,” and continuing for 28 days. Beyond 72 hours PEP is not advised. This strict timeline means that acting immediately versus waiting a night can produce completely different outcomes.
tips.sources: Beijing Municipal People's Government. Can't tell the difference between before and after? Six questions and six answers to comprehensively understand HIV pre-exposure/post-exposure prophylaxis. <https://www.beijing.gov.cn/fuwu/bmfw/jhsyfwzdzx/sjazbr/fakp/202311/t20231110_3299397.html>
tips.caveats: Many cities now offer 24‑hour clinics; in Chongqing, for example, 29 such clinics operate across 26 districts, 14 of which are open around the clock. Call the local CDC beforehand to find a clinic with PEP on hand — don’t waste time in the emergency room. Situations considered “exposures” include unprotected sex, a broken condom, needle sticks, or blood contact with mucous membranes; only a doctor can decide whether PEP is appropriate. The full 28‑day regimen must be completed; missing doses markedly reduces its effectiveness. Follow‑up testing is required at 4–6 weeks and at 3 months as directed by your physician. This is a remedial measure, not a substitute for regular prevention; for everyday safeguards and testing, see items 30 and 31 in Chapter 1 (consistent condom use and testing after high‑risk encounters).

tips.title: After an injury while helping, use the legal compensation routes — there is no automatic reimbursement fund
tips.cost: Emergency treatment at a government hospital is free or low cost. A private hospital bill is recoverable only through a claim.
tips.inPlainWords: If you are injured while saving someone, you may have a claim against the person who caused the danger, a claim under the Motor Vehicles Act for a road accident, or victim compensation under the BNSS, 2023. The Good Samaritan protection in section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act protects you from liability; it does not pay your bill. Keep the medical records and the police report.
tips.benefit: Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 protects a Good Samaritan from civil and criminal liability for helping a road-accident victim. The BNSS, 2023 provides victim compensation, and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 provides legal aid. A civil suit in tort can claim damages from the wrongdoer. A government hospital must provide emergency treatment.
tips.sources: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (section 134A). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Legal Services Authority. <https://nalsa.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A rescue does not create an automatic state-funded payout. Preserve the police report, the medical records and the witness details. A claim has a limitation period.

tips.title: Knives, rebar, glass piercing the body – apply pressure around the foreign object to stop bleeding; do not pull it out
tips.cost: No cost involved. The hard part is resisting the instinct to “pull it out” and instead staying with the injured person until help arrives.
tips.inPlainWords: Pulling out the object can cause severe bleeding and makes it harder for doctors to assess the extent of the injury. The correct approach is to call 112, then use your hand or a dressing to apply firm pressure around the object to control bleeding and keep it stable so it doesn’t move. If internal organs are visible through an abdominal wound, do not push them back in; simply cover them with a clean, moist dressing. For chest wounds where air bubbles are escaping, do not seal them with plastic wrap – doing so can cause the lung to collapse.
tips.benefit: The 2025 International First Aid Guidelines from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies state: “First aiders should apply pressure around any foreign object (such as a knife) that has penetrated the body and keep it stable; do not remove it.” “Never pull any object out of abdominal or chest wounds – doing so can cause severe bleeding and makes it harder to assess the injury.” “Foreign objects embedded in the body should be kept stable; if they move with the pulse, simply hold them gently in place.” “First aiders must not push protruding organs back into the body.” For open chest wounds with active bleeding, “it is acceptable to leave them uncovered, as sealing them may trap air in the chest cavity and cause partial or total lung collapse (pneumothorax).” All penetrating abdominal or chest injuries require immediate emergency care.
tips.sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2025). International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025, pp. 256–257, 267–268. <https://www.ifrc.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/IFRC%20International%20First%20Aid,%20Resuscitation%20and%20Education%20Guidelines%202025.pdf>; National Disaster Management Authority. <https://ndma.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: This grade is assigned because these actions are widely accepted in official guidelines; however, no randomized trials exist, and it would be unethical to randomly assign patients to “remove” versus “not remove” such objects. The sole exception is when a foreign object blocks the airway and prevents breathing. In such cases, go directly to the emergency triage desk at the hospital and state “penetrating injury.” This falls under the highest priority category – do not wait in line at the registration desk (see Section 24, Item 8). If a penetrating injury occurs, call 112; the ambulance will alert the hospital in advance. For techniques on controlling severe bleeding and applying tourniquets, see Section 12.

tips.title: If a fracture is suspected, don’t move the injured area — keep it supported and apply cold for up to 20 minutes; never try to realign it yourself.
tips.cost: No cost involved. Use a stiff board, rolled‑up magazines, or clothing as a splint. Wrap cold items in a cloth before applying them.
tips.inPlainWords: Any injury to a limb should be treated as a possible fracture at first — being able to stand or move does not rule it out; only an X‑ray can confirm it. Keep the injured part still, supporting it with your hand or using a triangular bandage or rigid splint to hold it in its original position. Apply cold as soon as possible, but never for more than 20 minutes at a time. Do not attempt to realign the bone yourself. For open fractures where bone pierces the skin, first stop any bleeding and cover the wound with a clean dressing; do not push the bone back into place.
tips.benefit: The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies released its 2025 International First Aid Guidelines, which state that “any injury to a limb should be treated as a possible fracture” and “the only reliable way to confirm a fracture is an X‑ray; when in doubt, treat it as a fracture.” The purpose of immobilisation is “to minimise movement and pain.” Cold application “should be limited to 20 minutes at a time to reduce pain; longer exposure can damage the skin.” “For long bones such as the femur, bleeding from the bone itself can be life‑threatening.” Call emergency services if there is significant pain or swelling, signs of shock, a suspected femoral fracture, or obvious deformity of the limb. Only under two specific conditions may a fractured bone be manually realigned on site: first, when help is far away (or resources are limited) and the part of the limb below the angle appears cold and pale, or when the rescuer cannot safely immobilise it for transport; second, only if the rescuer is properly trained. For open fractures, the priority is stopping bleeding and preventing infection.
tips.sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2025). International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025, pp. 301–302. <https://www.ifrc.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/IFRC%20International%20First%20Aid,%20Resuscitation%20and%20Education%20Guidelines%202025.pdf>
tips.caveats: This grade B rating reflects that these practices are widely accepted. There is only one older study supporting the use of traction immobilisation for femoral fractures before hospital care; its reliability is low, yet it shows modest benefits such as reduced blood loss within 24 hours, shorter hospital stays, and no meaningful difference in mortality or complications. No evidence exists regarding whether early realignment yields any advantage over simple immobilisation. Three common misconceptions should be corrected: being able to walk does not rule out a fracture; cold alone — not alternating hot and cold — is appropriate; and sprains do not “work themselves out” with movement; rest is essential. For elderly patients with suspected fractures after a fall, refer to item 2 for handling precautions. Swelling of one leg after casting or bed rest may indicate a clot; see item 11 for details. Information on disability assessment and eligibility for a disability certificate after treatment can be found in section 24, items 10 and 11.

tips.title: After sexual assault, go to a safe place and call 112; do not shower, wash clothes, or tidy the room before a medical exam, and visit a hospital within 72 hours.
tips.cost: Calling the police costs nothing. Emergency contraceptives are over-the-counter medicines available at any pharmacy. Post-exposure prophylaxis treatment costs over a thousand rupees per course; whether it is needed must be decided by a doctor — see item 38 in this section regarding obtaining PEP within 72 hours. The real challenge is that it is extremely hard to speak up at the moment, and many victims simply want to take a shower right away.
tips.inPlainWords: Physical traces on the body, on clothing, and in the room are the most crucial evidence for identifying the perpetrator. Therefore, avoid showering, washing clothes, or cleaning the area before a medical exam, and call 112 as soon as possible. Emergency contraceptives are readily available at pharmacies and work best when taken early. Within 72 hours, visit a hospital so a doctor can determine if PEP is necessary.
tips.benefit: Prosecutors from the Beijing People’s Procuratorate state: “Whether minors or adults, anyone who experiences sexual assault should call 112 immediately.” Prompt reporting and medical care “allow investigators to examine the scene, collect physical evidence, and preserve proof in a timely manner.” A sexual assault prevention guide published by the Guizhou Provincial Civil Affairs Bureau and reprinted by People’s Daily advises: “If sexual assault occurs, preserving evidence is the top priority.” It recommends keeping “body fluids, hair, skin cells, and communication records” and warns that “after an assault, one must not shower, wash clothes, tidy the room, or throw anything away.” In cases involving acquaintances, preserving call logs and messages is essential; any threats or attempts at bribery by the perpetrator must also be documented. The Xicheng District Procuratorate in Beijing adds: “Try not to shower before undergoing a physical examination.” WHO notes that emergency contraception may be used “when a woman has been sexually assaulted without effective contraceptive protection,” recommending its use within five days for maximum effectiveness. According to the Wuhan Health Commission, “the sooner these pills are taken after unprotected intercourse — ideally within 72 hours — the better they prevent pregnancy.” PEP for HIV should be taken within two hours if possible, and no later than 72 hours.

The main beneficiaries are the victim herself and her family. These pills have no effect if pregnancy has already occurred. When reporting to police, provide a truthful account without exaggeration or concealment. Any attempts by the perpetrator to settle privately, pay compensation, or threaten you must be documented and never deleted. You may decide to wait before calling police, but be aware that evidence deteriorates over time. Regardless of whether you call police, seek medical care within the stipulated timeframe. Recordings related to this topic are discussed in item 41 of section 8. If the perpetrator later uses photos or police reports to blackmail you, this also constitutes a crime — see item 32 of section 8. If a friend experiences sexual assault, accompany her to report it and to the hospital; do not suggest she shower or rest first.

tips.title: When a baby under 1 year is choking and cannot cry out, alternate 5 back blows (face-down) and 5 chest thrusts — never press the belly
tips.cost: No cost. Watch a demonstration once or take a short infant first-aid class — a few minutes to half a day. The hard part is staying calm enough to turn the baby face-down on your forearm.
tips.inPlainWords: If the child can still cough or cry audibly, let them cough while you watch closely. If they cannot cry, their face turns blue, call 112, lay the baby face-down on your forearm, and give 5 back blows with the heel of your hand between the shoulder blades. If that fails, roll them over and give 5 quick thrusts on the center of the chest. Keep alternating — never push on the belly. If the baby becomes unresponsive, switch to CPR.
tips.benefit: The American Heart Association and American Academy of Pediatrics issued 2025 pediatric basic life support guidance. It states that choking (for example, an object blocking the airway) “is a leading cause of death in infants and children.” Liquids are what infants most often aspirate. Mild obstruction: still coughing or making sounds — let the child cough while you monitor for worsening. Severe obstruction: weak cough or none, cannot cry, cyanosis — call emergency services first, then “repeat cycles of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object is expelled or the infant becomes unresponsive.” Abdominal thrusts are not recommended for infants because they can injure internal organs. Chest thrusts are now taught with the heel of one hand because it achieves greater depth than the old two-finger method. When the infant is unresponsive, start CPR with compressions first; do not check a pulse. Remove only visible objects before giving breaths. The guideline explicitly says “do not perform blind finger sweeps.” The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies 2025 international first-aid guidance uses the same sequence: up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then turn the infant and give up to 5 chest thrusts, then call emergency services if needed. Its chest-thrust technique uses a two-thumb encircling grip. The Fujian Provincial Red Cross emergency-care training center describes “5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts” for infants under 1 year: hold the infant prone on the forearm with the head lower than the trunk for back blows.

Benefit is rated large by judgment: a fully blocked airway can stop an infant’s heart within minutes. The main beneficiaries are your own children. For children 1 year and older and adults, use abdominal thrusts; see item 26 in this section (choking: back blows plus abdominal thrusts). The 2025 U.S. guideline dropped two-finger compressions because depth was inadequate. Any of these beats doing nothing. Even after the object is expelled, seek medical care — fragments may remain in the lungs. Keep coins and small toys out of reach. If the baby is unresponsive, see item 44 in this section (infant CPR).

tips.title: If a baby under 1 is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call 112 on speakerphone and perform infant CPR: 30 compressions, then 2 breaths
tips.cost: No cost. Infant CPR takes one hands-on class, half a day to a full day. The hard parts are sealing your mouth over the infant’s mouth and nose for breaths and pressing firmly enough.
tips.inPlainWords: No response to foot stimulation and no normal breathing — call 112 on speakerphone and do not stop. Encircle the chest with both hands and compress with two thumbs; if you cannot encircle, use the heel of one hand, about 4 cm (1.5 inches) deep, about 2 compressions per second. After every 30 compressions, give 2 breaths covering mouth and nose. Most infant cardiac arrests start with breathing failure; CPR that includes breaths improves survival.
tips.benefit: The American Heart Association and American Academy of Pediatrics 2025 pediatric basic life support guideline states that respiratory problems remain the main cause of cardiac arrest in infants and children. Among infants with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, only 6.6% survive to hospital discharge. For an unresponsive infant or child with abnormal breathing and no signs of life, “CPR should be started immediately” without checking a pulse. Compression depth is at least one-third of the anteroposterior chest diameter; for infants, “about 1.5 inches (4 cm).” Rate 100 to 120 per minute. One rescuer: 30 compressions then 2 breaths. Two rescuers: 15 compressions then 2 breaths. Use one-hand heel or two-thumb encircling compressions; if encircling is not possible, use heel of one hand. Two-finger compression has been removed because depth was inadequate. The guideline also states that for out-of-hospital pediatric cardiac arrest, adding ventilations to compressions improves survival. A U.S. registry of 3,900 children under 18 with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest found 59.4% were infants. Bystander CPR was associated with an adjusted hospital discharge survival of 13.2% versus 9.5% without CPR; adjusted OR 1.57 (about 57% higher odds of survival), 95% CI 1.25–1.96. Among infants, CPR with breaths was linked to higher survival and better neurological recovery; compression-only outcomes were similar to no CPR. IFRC 2025 guidance: check responsiveness by picking up the infant or flicking the foot. If alone, call emergency services on speakerphone. If no phone allows simultaneous calling, perform 1 minute of CPR before calling. A popular-science article from the Capital Institute of Pediatrics, republished by the Beijing Municipal Health Commission, states: “If only 1 person is present, perform 2 minutes of CPR before calling 120.” Compression depth “4 cm for infants.” Mouth-to-mouth-nose for breaths under 1 year.

tips.title: If a child swallows a button battery or two or more powerful rare-earth magnets, proceed immediately to an emergency department equipped for endoscopy: do not induce vomiting or wait for bowel passage
tips.cost: Zero financial outlay for prevention; emergency diagnostic X-rays and endoscopic/surgical removal incur standard clinical hospital fees. At home, screw battery compartments tightly shut on TV remotes, electronic scales, key fobs, and children's toys, and lock spare coin batteries and neodymium magnetic spheres far out of reach. The difficulty is that button battery ingestions are unwitnessed in the majority of cases, and children often appear completely asymptomatic initially.
tips.inPlainWords: A button battery lodged in the esophagus can generate caustic electrical burns that cause irreversible necrosis within 2 hours, even while the child appears cheerful. Two or more swallowed rare-earth magnets attract each other across bowel loops, pinching tissue until the intestine perforates. If ingestion is even suspected, rush immediately to an emergency hospital for radiographic localization. Never induce vomiting, never wait for it to pass in stool, and never wait for symptoms to manifest.
tips.benefit: Data from the National Poison Data System spanning 1985 to 2009 showed a 6.7-fold increase in the percentage of button battery ingestions resulting in major injury or fatality. The greatest danger stems from 20 mm diameter lithium coin cells (such as CR2032). Children under age 4 swallowing >=20 mm cells experience disproportionately catastrophic clinical outcomes. Lodged in the esophagus, a battery generates an electrical current that hydrolyzes tissue fluids into concentrated sodium hydroxide, causing severe liquefaction necrosis with lifelong sequelae in as little as 2 to 2.5 hours. In fatal cases, 92% of ingestions were unwitnessed; among major injuries, 56% were unwitnessed. At least 54% of fatal cases and 27% of severe morbidity cases were initially misdiagnosed due to non-specific initial symptoms. Furthermore, injury progression continues deeply after battery extraction; esophageal perforation, tracheoesophageal fistula, aortoesophageal fistula, and fatal exsanguination have occurred days post-removal. In an analysis of 8,648 cases, 61.8% of batteries swallowed by children under 6 were extracted directly by the child from household battery-powered electronics. National Capital Poison Center guidelines instruct: if battery ingestion is suspected, "do not induce vomiting"; lodged batteries cause severe burns "in as little as 2 hours" and "do not wait for symptoms to develop." All patients under 12 years require immediate emergency X-ray imaging. Surveillance data from Guangdong CDC revealed nearly 100 pediatric battery ingestions over 5 years (92.9% involving children aged 0–6, with 39.3% sustaining moderate-to-severe injuries and 25.0% requiring inpatient hospitalization), mandating immediate emergency care and cautioning against home-induced emesis. When multiple neodymium magnet balls (e.g. Buckyballs) are swallowed, magnetic attraction clamps adjacent bowel segments, causing ischemia, bowel necrosis, intestinal obstruction, and perforation. A 2025 systematic review of 130 children who developed entero-enteric fistulas from multiple magnet ingestion found a median age of 3.3 years, with 95.5% requiring major surgical laparotomy, 19% developing postoperative complications, and 1 fatality.

Benefit is categorized as High because coin cells cause fatal esophageal erosion within 2 hours, and mortality is concentrated in unwitnessed and delayed-diagnosis cases. Beneficiaries are predominantly young children. When transporting the child, bring an identical battery sample, product packaging, or the opened device to assist emergency physicians in rapid radiographic size identification. Guidance regarding pre-hospital oral honey administration differs between jurisdictions: National Capital Poison Center suggests giving 10 mL of pure honey every 10 minutes (up to 6 doses) if the child is >=1 year old, ingestion occurred <12 hours prior, the child can swallow, and honey is immediately at hand, based on ex vivo porcine models demonstrating that honey buffers alkaline burns. Never delay hospital transit to search for honey. If a battery is ingested concurrently with a magnet, poison centers mandate urgent endoscopic removal even if it has reached the stomach. The elderly are also vulnerable: 15.5% of 8,648 recorded ingestions involved adults mistaking batteries (predominantly 36.3% hearing aid button cells) for oral prescription pills. For acute airway obstruction, see Chapter 13, Rule 26 (back blows and abdominal thrusts) or Rule 43 (infant choking). tips.title: If someone is severely intoxicated, place them in the recovery position and maintain continuous observation without leaving them alone: call emergency services immediately if unarousable, breathing abnormally, seizing, or hypothermic
tips.cost: Zero monetary cost. Care requires several hours of vigilant physical observation, often lasting through the night. The challenge is remaining alert when you have consumed alcohol yourself, resisting the urge to go home to sleep, and overcoming the pervasive cultural myth that an intoxicated person simply needs to "sleep it off."
tips.inPlainWords: An intoxicated person who loses consciousness can choke to death on their own vomitus or suffer respiratory arrest. Place them on their side in the recovery position and keep someone stationed beside them continuously; never abandon them to sleep alone in a closed room. Call emergency services immediately if they cannot be awakened, breathe slowly or irregularly (<8 breaths/min or >10-second pauses), seize, or develop cold, clammy, cyanotic skin. Never force coffee, never put them in a cold shower, and never induce vomiting.
tips.benefit: NHS clinical guidelines list key signs of acute alcohol poisoning: severe mental confusion, slurred speech, loss of coordination, vomiting, incontinence, pale or bluish/clammy skin, slow or irregular respiration, seizures, and unresponsiveness. If alcohol poisoning is suspected, or the individual is unconscious or stops breathing, immediately call emergency services. Core action protocol: remain by their side continuously because they risk suffocating on vomit or experiencing respiratory depression; keep awake individuals seated upright; place unconscious breathing individuals into the lateral recovery position; offer small sips of water only if fully conscious and able to swallow; and keep them warm with coats or blankets. Five critical contraindications: (1) never give more alcohol; (2) never feed food, which induces airway aspiration; (3) never administer coffee or caffeinated drinks, which worsen dehydration; (4) never put them under a cold shower or in a cold bath, which precipitates severe hypothermia, falls, or drowning; and (5) never attempt to induce vomiting. Emergency department clinical data published by Shaanxi Provincial Health Commission highlight that alcohol depresses laryngeal protective reflexes, making vomitus easily aspirated into trachea and bronchial trees, causing asphyxiation and immediate death; emergency teams frequently recover intoxicated individuals already in fatal cardiac arrest packed with pulmonary aspiration debris. In stuporous or comatose stages marked by cyanosis, cold extremities, hypothermia, and shallow breathing, call emergency services immediately, maintain a lateral position without emesis, apply warm blankets, and initiate CPR immediately if breathing ceases. Beijing Municipal Health Commission advises: "Never let an intoxicated individual sleep alone to avoid unmonitored asphyxiation." CDC statistics indicate an average of 2,221 annual alcohol poisoning deaths among individuals aged 15 and older in the United States (roughly 6 deaths per day).

Benefit is categorized as High because asphyxiation and respiratory arrest occur almost exclusively when victims are left unmonitored. Never attempt manual throat-tickling emesis on lethargic or unresponsive individuals. Beyond family members, these duties apply heavily to dining companions and colleagues: under tort law, co-drinkers share affirmative legal duties of reasonable care and safety. In Jiangsu Taixing, co-drinkers who failed to notify family or escort an incapacitated colleague home before he drowned in a river were held liable for 7% and 3% comparative fault (apportioning ₹14,76,200 in damages). Always escort drunk companions directly into the custody of family or remain until sobriety returns. If discovering an unknown intoxicated person collapsed outdoors, call emergency dispatchers without attempting forceful repositioning unless necessary (see Chapter 13, Rule 2). Alcohol impairs thermoregulation; manage hypothermia as outlined in Chapter 13, Rule 28. Alcohol interactions with cephalosporin or metronidazole antibiotics causing disulfiram-like reactions are detailed in Chapter 34, Rule 11. Never take hot baths or enter saunas after drinking (see Chapter 22, Rule 11).

tips.title: If a finger or toe is severed, compress the wound to stop bleeding, wrap the amputated part in damp sterile gauze inside a sealed plastic bag immersed in ice water, and transport immediately to a specialized hand surgery hospital
tips.cost: Zero financial cost for emergency preservation; emergency microvascular replantation and hospital treatment incur specialized surgical costs. Maintain sterile gauze and zip-top plastic bags in household first-aid kits. The psychological challenge is prioritizing patient hemostasis over the detached digit, and refraining from placing the severed part directly into water or bare ice.
tips.inPlainWords: First apply direct firm pressure to the stump wound to halt bleeding and call emergency services. Wrap the severed digit in clean damp gauze, place it into a waterproof sealed plastic bag, and submerge the sealed bag in an ice-water slurry. Never let the severed digit touch ice directly and never immerse it unbagged in liquid. Without cold preservation, warm ischemia limits replantation viability to roughly 4 to 6 hours. With proper preservation, over 80% of replanted digits survive.
tips.benefit: MedlinePlus emergency protocols instruct: apply direct manual pressure to the amputation site to arrest hemorrhage and elevate the injured extremity; apply a tourniquet only for life-threatening arterial bleeding unresponsive to direct pressure. Recover and preserve every severed anatomical fragment to accompany the patient. If contaminated, rinse the severed part gently. Wrap the severed digit in a clean damp cloth or sterile saline gauze, seal it inside a waterproof plastic bag, and submerge the sealed bag in an ice-water bath. Crucial contraindications: (1) never submerge the body part directly in water or ice without a sealed bag; (2) never place severed tissue directly in contact with ice cubes; (3) never use dry ice, which causes irreversible frostbite cryo-necrosis; and (4) in the absence of ice, keep the part as cool as possible and insulated from ambient heat. Cold ischemia dramatically extends tissue viability; uncooled amputated digits tolerate warm ischemia for only approximately 4 to 6 hours before microvascular thrombi and muscle necrosis prevent successful revascularization. Never assume an amputated fragment is too mangled or small to salvage, and never attempt to shove protruding bone back into the stump. American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) guidelines emphasize prompt transit to trauma centers with 24/7 on-call microvascular hand surgery capabilities. A 2024 systematic review of 31 clinical studies evaluating 2,276 digits demonstrated an overall replantation survival rate of 86.8% (1,976 successful salvages vs. 300 failures); among 1,087 patients undergoing replantation, 82.9% successfully returned to employment. A meta-analysis of 12 studies reported an 85.3% digit survival rate. Another meta-analysis across 12 studies and 3,645 patients identified total ischemic time >=8 hours as a critical risk factor for postoperative microvascular necrosis, with odds of replantation failure 2.25 times higher (OR 2.25, 95% CI: 1.43–3.54).

tips.caveats: Graded Evidence Grade B because preservation standards reflect international emergency surgery guidelines and observational surgical cohort registries rather than randomized controlled trials. Benefit magnitude is categorized as Moderate: intervention salvages functional limbs rather than saving life. Replantation feasibility is determined by surgical teams based on injury morphology; clean guillotine cuts carry vastly higher replantation success than severe crush or avulsion injuries. Saving life always precedes saving limbs: secure hemostasis on the stump before packaging severed tissue. For tourniquet application under uncontrolled hemorrhage, see Chapter 13, Rule 12. Angle grinder safety guards to prevent traumatic hand amputations are detailed in Chapter 1, Rule 42. Primary beneficiaries are manual laborers, machine operators, and household cooks.

tips.title: If a permanent tooth is completely knocked out, hold it by the crown, gently rinse it, reinsert it into the socket immediately if possible, or submerge it in milk and seek immediate dental emergency care; never reinsert a baby tooth
tips.cost: Zero financial cost for first-aid preservation; subsequent dental repositioning, splinting, and endodontic care incur clinical fees. Whole milk or sterile saline is readily available in homes or nearby convenience stores. The psychological barrier is overcoming squeamishness to push an avulsed tooth back into an open bleeding socket, and correctly distinguishing an adult permanent tooth from a deciduous baby tooth.
tips.inPlainWords: Handle the knocked-out tooth strictly by its white crown and never touch the root surface. If dirty, rinse gently with milk or sterile saline; if possible, reinsert it immediately into its socket and gently bite down on a clean cloth. If reinsertion fails, submerge the tooth in a cup of cold milk and see a dentist immediately; never wrap it in dry tissue paper. Immediate replantation carries only a ~17% long-term root ankylosis rate, whereas teeth left dry for over an hour suffer over 85% ankylosis. Baby teeth must never be replanted.
tips.benefit: NHS emergency guidance for a knocked-out tooth dictates: hold the tooth strictly by the crown (the white portion visible above the gumline) without contacting the root surface. If contaminated, rinse gently in milk, saline, or saliva. Attempt to reinsert the tooth back into its socket; if successful, bite gently on a clean tissue or handkerchief to hold it steady and visit an emergency dentist immediately. If reinsertion is impossible, transport the tooth submerged in milk or buccal saliva. Baby teeth (deciduous teeth) must never be replanted as reinsertion damages the underlying developing permanent tooth bud. The International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) "Save a Tooth" protocols outline identical steps: retrieve tooth, handle only by crown, rinse briefly under cold tap water if dirty, and choose one of three storage methods: (1) immediate replantation into socket; (2) immersion in a glass of cold milk or physiological saline; or (3) transport held between cheek and gum (buccal sulcus), followed by immediate dental transit. A long-term clinical database study from Copenhagen University Hospital tracking 145 avulsed permanent teeth in 116 patients followed for 7 months to 23 years evaluated the risk of replacement resorption (ankylosis, where root cementum fuses to alveolar bone and is gradually resorbed): teeth replanted immediately showed a 17.2% ankylosis rate; teeth stored in physiological wet media (saliva/saline) prior to replantation showed 55.3%; and teeth left in dry storage for >=60 minutes exhibited an 85.7% ankylosis rate. An earlier cohort of 400 avulsed teeth re-evaluated in 2020 revealed that for immature teeth with open apices, dry storage <20 minutes carried a 33.9% ankylosis risk, rising to 60.0% past 60 minutes; for mature teeth with closed apices, ankylosis escalated from 59.4% to 86.4% at 900 days. Tap water storage for >20 minutes caused widespread periodontal ligament necrosis and root resorption. Overall, 30% of avulsed teeth eventually required extraction during long-term follow-up.

tips.caveats: Graded Evidence Grade B because statistics stem from longitudinal specialized dental hospital trauma registries without prospective randomized arms. Benefit is categorized as Moderate because tooth preservation preserves dentition aesthetics and masticatory function rather than preventing mortality. Researchers emphasize that even teeth experiencing prolonged dry storage (>60 min) should not be discarded, as specialized endodontic splinting and chemical treatments still salvage a proportion of teeth or maintain alveolar ridge volume for future implants. Tap water should only be used for a brief 10-second rinse; never transport teeth immersed in tap water due to hypotonic cell lysis. Primary beneficiaries are active children and adults prone to sports impacts, falls, and cycling collisions. In cases of unrecoverable tooth loss, removable partial dentures can bridge the gap during childhood until definitive adult dental bridges or endosseous implants are placed (see Chapter 24, Rule 12 for dental implant bundled pricing).
